Many people think of mental health only as a diagnosis, but psychotherapist and mental health advocate Tala Al Kurd invites a different view: well-being as a daily way of life. She shows how care and resilience have long been woven into culture through language, music, art, and faith, and how recognizing those roots can help reduce stigma and support a more balanced, human approach to mental health. Tala Al Kurd holds an MA in Psychotherapy and Counselling and a Postgraduate Diploma in Education. For the past 13 years, she has taught IBDP Psychology and for 8 years has served as Extended Essay Coordinator. description: Is the stress you carry home a personal failure, or a hidden wound from modern work culture? Learn to move past the "endurance" mindset and adopt a new model of recovery to regulate your nervous system and reclaim your wellbeing. What if microbes could solve one of the world's biggest crises? We're drowning in e-waste, shipping our old electronics overseas to be burned in open air and losing billions in precious metals in the process. 

In this fascinating TEDxManchester Talk, scientist and co-founder of Lanthagen, Sahara Bhanot, reveals how her team is using microbes to extract rare earth elements from electronic waste, slashing our reliance on foreign supply chains and turning toxic junk into liquid gold. The future of mining isn't underground; it's biological. Dr Sahara Bhanot is a biotechnologist, entrepreneur, and Co-Founder & Chief Scientific Officer (CSO) of LanthaGen Bio, a startup focused on developing sustainable, synthetic biology-based rare earth metal extraction systems.

She holds a BSc in Chemistry and an MPhil in Biotechnology from the University of Manchester. She recently earned her PhD also at Manchester. Her doctoral research, sponsored by the Future Biomanufacturing Research Hub, involved
title: How biotech could scavenge rare earth minerals from e-waste | Sahara Bhanot | TEDxManchester

description: How comfortable would you be with a judge using an AI tool to help decide your court case? Today, judges often rely on AI tools to help them make decisions – from recommending sentences, to predicting risk in domestic violence cases, to drafting judgments. This is a seismic change in how justice is done. Stripping back a well-functioning judicial system to its 101 elements, legitimacy is a crucial building block. Where judges use AI, the public must have confidence in the fairness of court processes and outcomes, and view them as legitimate. This TEDx talk sets out a roadmap for legitimate AI in courts. The idea is straightforward: just as judges must follow principles of good conduct, AI tools must follow principles of good design. The roadmap has three key milestones achieved through stakeholder-led research. First, define principles to guide AI tools. title: Reimagining Justice: How to Build Legitimate AI for Judges | Brian Barry | TEDxTrinityCollegeDublin

author: TEDx Talks
description: Technicians are foundational to creation. Humans have made art for tens of thousands of years and parallel to that has been collaboration and commissions. We are familiar with the concept of workshops and craftspeople who create commissions of other people’s designs. But we only consider one, or very few, of the people involved in this process as artists. They are two sides of the same coin. If one person designs a set, the construction of the flats has to be worked out. If someone draws a lighting plan, someone has to devise how to make it work. If someone designs a sculpture, a team of people might figure out how to achieve it.  This creative problem-solving, where new technologies are tried and tested, is the other side, the hidden side, of that final product most of us see. Right now in Senegal the first generation of theatre and performance technicians are being trained in an art form that isn’t yet fully realised. This talk is about the potential of an artform to be rediscovered
title: Dublin to Dakar: How Technicians Make Great Art | Blú Hanley | TEDxTrinityCollegeDublin

description: We need the law to deliver justice, but what happens when it messes up? Bhadra Panicker shares the story of a woman falsely accused of killing her own child. Built on flawed evidence and systemic biases, this case resulted in an infamous miscarriage of justice and destroyed numerous lives forever. Yet, this tragedy shines a light on grave failures in the legal system - and reveal why real change actually starts with asking better questions. Bhadra Panicker is a Law and Business student at Trinity College Dublin. As a Laidlaw Scholar, she conducted research on miscarriages of justice against women, developing her passion for feminist jurisprudence. Her work combines academic work with practical engagement to platform conversations about achieving equality and empowerment in the law.
